content.summary_of_the_paper: The main contribution of the paper is an algorithm for learning from multiple domains with the goal to diminish the dependence on spurious (meaning domain-specific) features, and instead learn predictors that depend on features that are informative across the domains. The authors also do some analysis in the linear case, demonstrating failures of ERM.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
*Strengths*

The issues pointed out by the authors of doing ERM over the average loss over all domains are real, and assuming they have not been pointed out before, I think it’s interesting (I could not quite tell given the poor writing). The authors also point out limitations of previous approaches that zero out parts of the gradient in an axis-aligned way: I can see how zeroing our parts of the gradient can lead to poor performance and not actually improve multi-domain learning. Thus the authors seem to be solving an actual problem, and their proposed solution seems reasonable. I also liked that the authors analyzed a linear model and tried to demonstrate how their algorithm could lead to improved learning in a multi-domain setting, relying less on spurious features, and more on features that are useful for all domains.

*Weaknesses*

I would say one of the major issues is lack of clarity in mathematical notation, setup and results. Without writing down parts of the problem myself, I cannot even confirm that their linear model results are correct. Please see the issues listed under “Clarity” below. I encourage the authors to look at textbooks and previous papers for standard notation, state their main result in a “Theorem” format, and have a formal proof of the result, rather than some vague in-text intuition.

The paper is inundated with typos, which I find very distracting. As a reader, it makes me think that the authors rushed the work, and did not review it themselves, thus decreasing my trust in the work being technically correct.

The authors mention that for the linear case analysis once could use different losses. In general, it seems that the analysis is only interesting under early stopping, since in the convex case there is no difference among the solutions that average after learning on two domains, or learn for intervals, or learn simultaneously. This is not made clear.

Some of the claims made in the empirical results section are not substantiated. The authors present various hypothesis (e..g, SWAD may perform better than SDT in some cases, which is due to part of the training data relying on the same spurious features as the test data). It would be natural to evaluate such hypothesis and conjectures in at least a toy setting.

Some other questions: The algorithm itself consists of multiple components. The authors provide some ablations. The key component seems to be SWA. How does SWA alone perform? In general, SWA seems like a trick that the authors used, and little justification was provided for using this trick.

Section 5: How does using SWA find flatter minima? I would say it is backwards, and flatter minima may lead to success of SWA. Can the authors provide references for this claim? Or empirical analysis?

Recent work on model averaging is not discussed (branch-train-merge, model soups, etc). Such work is fairly recent, I suppose, so I am not judging the paper based on this, but the authors may want to familiarize themselves with the recent progress in model averaging, which also includes averaging across domains.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper lacks clarity: 
1) Poor notation. The notation is not standard and hard to follow. For example, after reading and re-reading, I believe R in Section 3 stands for reals. The standard notation is $\mathbb{R}$. Similarly, is $B$ meant to represent a set of binary values? The notation for features in 3.1 initially made me think that it is functions, since no actual definition was provided. Expectations are denoted by E instead of $\mathbb{E}$. These are just a few examples of notation and mathematical presentation issues.
2) Is D supposed to stand for the actual samples (data) or the distribution? Or the domain? I am not sure if the authors know themselves, given that in 3.1 they write “Training datasets are D_1 and D_2 and test domain is D_3.” Some conflicting information can be found throughout the text. The authors also take expectations over “(x,y) ~ D”, and I am note sure if it is supposed to mean an empirical average, or an actual expectation taken over (x,y) distributed according to D.
3) The only theorem in the paper is very informal, and basically computes the gradient of a linear model for subsets of the data. As a theorem, it is trivial. The only interesting part is in the paragraph below which is not stated as a theorem, nor is it formal.

I am confused how and why the authors used masking. It seems like it was important for the stability of the algorithm empirically. Related work sections pointed out that previous approaches used masking, and explained what issues it may lead to. But it seems like SDT also uses masking. What makes SDT truly unique and different, and not just a bag of tricks in one algorithm? 

I would suggest to have an explicit section or pseudocode to explain the algorithm (with all the tricks that are being used).

In the beginning of Section 3, the authors claim that they develop a framework. What framework is being developed? As I understand, the section introduces the setup and notation (partly, at least), and then looks at the linear model. What novel framework is being introduced?

The example given in Section 3.1 is quite nice, though _very_ poorly explained. Is it novel? I could not find differences between this example and the  one in Shi et al. ‘21. What new insights does it provide?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is poorly written, lacks mathematical clarity and precision, the so-called theoretical results are not stated in a formal matter. The mathematical analysis is straightforward. That said, if it was stated formally I would still count it as a contribution since it quite nicely illustrates the possible failures of ERM in multi-domain settings. The empirical results are lacking (lack of ablations, unjustified claims), and the proposed algorithm seems to be composed of several known algorithms. Once again, this latter issue would not be an issue if the algorithm was presented appropriately and explicitly (e.g., “we propose to combine X and Y which leads to improvements ABC” instead of suggesting that something incredibly novel is going on).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper investigates the effect of simplicity bias in domain generalization (DG) and then proposes the specific domain training (SDT) method to handle that issue. The main idea of STD is to reduce the effect of spurious features in settings. The experimental results show that SDT can produce better performance compared with some baseline methods in domain generalization.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Main questions for the authors:

1. Could you please give a formal (mathematical) definition of the simplicity bias in domain generalization?

2. Could you please provide a mathematical verification/guarantee for the claim about the benefit of SDT in learning domain-invariant features in domain generalization?

3. It is unclear to me the definition and the meaning of the $\rho$-spurious features in Eq. (2). Could the author please explain why the left-hand side of (2) can be considered as spurious features?
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, though I admit that the motivation and main ideas of the paper are relatively interesting, based on the assessment mentioned above, I think that the current manuscript is below the acceptance rate of an ICLR paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a simple method for learning classifiers that generalize well to unseen test domains using training data from multiple source domains. The method iterates learning a model using only one of the source domains for a predefined period while varying the target source domain; the authors believe that this training strategy will highlight weights for domain-invariant representation shared across diverse source domains while reducing the impact of weights relevant to domain-specific features. In addition, the method identifies weights for domain-invariant representation by comparing their loss gradients on a single source domain and those on the others, and accordingly updates weights dynamically. The proposed method was evaluated on multiple public benchmarks for domain generalization, on which it demonstrated decent performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strengths]
- The proposed method is simple to implement. 
- The advantage of the method was demonstrated empirically.

[Weaknesses]
- Some key assumptions of the paper are not fully justified, which makes me not convinced. The proposed method relies on the assumption that network weight parameters can be categorized into domain-invariant and spurious ones, but I am not sure whether this is feasible, in particular because those weights are interdependent. Unfortunately, there is no theoretical/empirical justification for this assumption. In addition, theorem 1 is derived only for a very specific and too simple classifier model, and there is no theoretical guarantee for the proposed method using modern machine learning models and conventional loss functions. 


- The current manuscript has many clarity issues, e.g., awkward sentences, grammar errors, bad organization (particularly in Section 3.3), errors on citation formats, and math notation issues. Hence, it looks like work in progress and I believe the writing quality is far below the standard of ICLR. 
- The paper has to discuss relations between the proposed method and previous work on debiased representation learning. Issues on spurious correlations between (domain-specific) latent attributes and target classes have been extensively studied and addressed for learning debiased models. Also, the proposed method looks relevant to debiasing methods using intentionally biased models to identify data with such spurious correlations. 
- I would recommend the authors to present connections between spurious correlations and domain generalization more clearly under realistic application scenarios (e.g., qualitative examples of spurious correlations that appear in real-world domain generalization problems). Figure 1 and related analysis are not useful in this context since they are too simple to reflect real domain generalization scenarios and are more appropriate for illustrating debiasing, not domain generalization. In my view, due to this issue and the motivation of this work presented in the manuscript, this work looks more like learning debiased models, but using multiple datasets with different bias attributes unlike the conventional setting of debiasing. 
- The simple simulation in Section 3.1 does not seem to be necessary since similar phenomenons have been investigated more rigorously and well known in the fields of debiasing (Learning from Failure, NeurIPS 2020) and shortcut learning (Which Shortcut Cues Will DNNs Choose? ICLR 2022). 
- Performance of the proposed method is not impressive. Further, it was not compared with latest approaches to domain generalization (e.g., those presented in CVPR 2022). It underperforms some of the recent work that is not reported in the paper. In addition, I would recommend the authors to evaluate their method on DomainBed.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Clarity and reproducibility: As mentioned above, this paper has many issues that damage readability and reproducibility significantly. Hence, it looks like an incomplete work and its writing quality is far below the standard of ICLR. 
- Novelty and quality: The paper seems to have potential since the main idea of this paper sounds reasonable and original. However, it is not fully convincing since its key assumptions are not well justified and its performance is not impressive. Thus, the quality of this paper is not satisfactory at present.
content.summary_of_the_review: The major weaknesses of the paper include lack of justification for the proposed method, lack of experiments, limited performance improvement, and low quality of presentation. For these reasons, although the proposed method sounds reasonable and has potential, I believe the paper does not meet the standard of ICLR and thus recommend rejection.

content.title: SDT: Specific Domain Training in Domain Generalization
content.TL;DR: we discern the spurious features by specific domain training.
content.abstract: Domain generalization (DG) methods aim to achieve generalizability to an unseen target domain by using only training data from the source domains. Although there has been a growing interest to learn from multiple training domains by applying different types of invariance across those domains, the improvements compared to empirical risk minimization (ERM) are almost negligible under controlled evaluation protocols. In this paper, we demonstrate that the disentanglement of spurious and invariant features is a tough task in standard training, since ERM simply minimize the loss and does not exploit invariance among domains. To address the issue, we introduce a simple yet effective method called specific domain training (SDT), which intensifies the trace of spurious features and make them more discernible and exploit masking strategy to decrease their effect. We provide a theoretical and experimental evidence to show the effectiveness of SDT for out-of-distribution generalization. Notably, SDT outperforms previous state of the art \citet{cha2021swad} in DomainNet benchmarks 0.2pp in average. Furthermore, SDT improves accuracy of some domains such as Sketch in PACS, SUN09 in VLCS and L100 in TerraIncognita by clear margins 2.5pp, 3.4pp, and 5.4pp respectively.
